1373.title: Three canons
1373.hook: the Pali canon, the Chinese canon and the Tibetan canon
1373.howItsDone: Theravada communities study and chant from the Pali canon, East Asian Buddhists draw on the Chinese canon, and Tibetan and Himalayan Buddhists use the Kangyur and Tengyur, often keeping the volumes wrapped in cloth on the temple shelf.

segments.voice: Yesterday, sudden and gradual: two verses on a wall, a slow ocean floor, and Bahiya freed in the street. Your line was both are true.

Near the end of his life, in the Pali account of his last days, the Buddha sees a worry coming. When he is gone, someone will say: our teacher is finished, we have no teacher anymore. Not so, he tells Ananda. The teaching and the discipline he has given them will be their teacher. So the monks did what people do with a teacher they cannot afford to lose. They remembered. They recited together. Later, the words were written down, and in different lands the remembering took different shapes.
screen: `WE HAVE NO TEACHER.` → `NOT SO.` → `THE TEACHING WILL BE YOUR TEACHER.`

segments.voice: A canon is a collection a community treats as its scripture. Buddhists keep three great ones, each in its own language, each with its own shape. First, the Pali canon, kept by the Theravada schools of Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia. Its name is the Tipitaka, which tradition explains as three baskets: one for the monastic discipline, one for the discourses, one for the higher teaching called Abhidhamma. Theravada tradition says it was handed down by memory for a long time before it was written. Second, the Chinese canon, sometimes called the great storehouse of scriptures. It holds texts translated from Indian languages, including collections of early discourses called the Agamas, which run close to the Pali ones: lay the two side by side and you find the same story, told with small differences. It also holds Mahayana sutras, monastic codes, and works first written in China, such as yesterday's Platform Sutra. It was read across China, Korea, Japan and Vietnam. Third, the Tibetan canon, which you met in year three, in two parts. The Kangyur gathers what Tibetan tradition counts as the Buddha's own word, in translation. The Tengyur gathers commentaries and treatises by later Indian teachers. Tibetan translators worked closely from Indian texts. The three overlap far more than their covers suggest. A monk in Bangkok, a nun in Taipei and a lama in Dharamsala can each open their own canon and find the Buddha teaching the four truths. The wording differs. The bookshelves differ.

segments.voice: Name the three canons quietly, one to a breath: the Pali, read this morning in a monastery in Sri Lanka or Thailand; the Chinese, a page turning in Seoul or Kyoto; the Tibetan, a long cloth-wrapped book being unwrapped on a table. Then sit with the thought the Buddha left Ananda: the teaching itself as the teacher.
Three canons. The Pali, the Chinese and the Tibetan collections of scripture, each its own library, often holding the same teachings in different words. Today's word.
Your line: three canons. The teacher, in the Buddha's own sense, is the same. Until tomorrow.

1374.title: Four languages
1374.hook: Pali, Sanskrit, Chinese, Tibetan: the teaching's great languages
1374.howItsDone: Theravada monasteries chant in Pali, East Asian temples chant sutras in Chinese or in local readings of Chinese, and Tibetan communities chant and study in Tibetan, while Buddhists also learn the teaching in their own everyday languages.

segments.voice: Yesterday, three canons: the Pali, the Chinese and the Tibetan, three shelves holding one teacher. Your line was three canons.

The complaint comes from a pair of brothers in robes. Born brahmins, both of them, with fine speaking voices. Monks of every name and clan and family have joined the order, they say, and each one repeats the Buddha's words in his own way of talking. The words are getting spoiled. Their solution: put the whole teaching into the old, formal verse of the Vedas, the learned language of priests. Fixed, polished, safe. It's a reasonable request. And the Buddha says no.
screen: `TWO BROTHERS COMPLAIN.` → `PUT IT IN THE PRIESTS' VERSE.` → `THE BUDDHA SAYS NO.`

segments.voice: That story is from the monastic rules called the Cullavagga. The Buddha rebukes the brothers, then gives a permission: the monks may learn his word in its own language. Readers have taken that line two ways. Some read it as each monk's own language. The old commentator Buddhaghosa read it as the Buddha's own speech, which Theravada tradition calls Magadhi and identifies with Pali. The text doesn't settle it. Either way, the teaching would not be locked in the priests' tongue. So it traveled. First, Pali, which Theravada monasteries still chant at morning and evening services. Second, Sanskrit, in which Mahayana sutras and great Indian treatises were kept, and from which Tibetan and Chinese translators often worked. Third, Chinese. Translators labored to find Chinese words for Indian ideas; the monk Kumarajiva's versions are still chanted in East Asian temples. Fourth, Tibetan, into which teams of translators carried Indian texts with great care over terms. Hear it in one word. In Pali and Sanskrit, buddha, the awakened one. In Chinese, fo, one short syllable. In Tibetan, sangye, which Tibetan tradition says joins two ideas: cleared of what obscures, and blossomed into full knowing. One person, many sounds. Each language also changed what people heard: a Chinese reader and a Tibetan reader meet the Buddha through different pictures. Learning a word from each is a way of visiting their homes.
screen: `HIS WORD IN ITS OWN LANGUAGE.` · `PALI AND SANSKRIT.` · `CHINESE AND TIBETAN.` · `BUDDHA, FO, SANGYE.` · then, large: `MANY TONGUES.`

segments.voice: On an out-breath, say softly: buddha, the awakened one, in Pali and Sanskrit. On the next, try fo, the Chinese, or sangye, the Tibetan, whichever sits easier in your mouth, and go back and forth a few times, slowly. Then let the words go quiet, and sit with all the mouths that have said this one name in their own way.
Four languages. Pali, Sanskrit, Chinese and Tibetan: the great languages that carried the teaching, each giving the Buddha's word its own sound. Today's word.
Your line: many tongues. The schools you've met this month live, in part, inside their languages. See you tomorrow.

options: No. He refused the brothers' Vedic verse, and the teaching spread into many languages.
Yes. He asked that it be kept in the Vedas' formal verse, like priests' texts.
Yes. He chose Sanskrit alone, so every translation since breaks his rule.
chat.meaning: In the Cullavagga the Buddha refuses to lock his word in Vedic verse; it traveled into Pali, Sanskrit, Chinese and Tibetan.

1375.title: Robes and colors
1375.hook: saffron in Thailand, maroon in Tibet, gray or black in Korea and Japan
1375.howItsDone: Monks and nuns in each school wear robes of a set color and cut, often sewn in a patchwork of strips; Theravada robes run from saffron to brown, Tibetan robes are maroon and yellow, and Korean and Japanese robes are often gray or black, sometimes with a small rakusu.

segments.voice: Yesterday, four languages: buddha, fo, sangye, one person in many sounds. Your line was many tongues.

Rice fields, seen from higher ground in Magadha. Long strips of green, low earth banks running between them, short banks crossing those, the whole plain laid out like a grid. In the monastic rules, the Buddha is walking with Ananda, and he stops to look at that view. Then he asks a tailor's question. Could Ananda make robes for the monks like that? A farmer's field, cut and sewn into cloth, and worn on the shoulder. That pattern is still there today, under robes of very different colors.
screen: `THE FIELDS OF MAGADHA.` → `A TAILOR'S QUESTION.` → `A FIELD ON THE SHOULDER.`

segments.voice: First, the field. That story is in the Mahavagga, part of the monastic rules. Ananda says he can make such robes, and does: cloth cut in pieces and sewn back together in rows, like a field seen from a hill. Robes today still often carry that patchwork, even when the cloth could have been one piece. Next, the dye. The old word for the robe's color is kashaya in Sanskrit, kasava in Pali: a dyed, earthy color, not a bright one. The rules ask monks to dye their cloth and avoid certain showy colors. The point was a robe that said: this person has stepped out of the market of fashion. Then the robe traveled, and the color shifted. In Thailand, Sri Lanka and Myanmar, robes range from saffron to ochre to a dark forest brown. In Tibet, maroon, with yellow for certain ceremonies and teachers. In Korea, gray. In Japan, black is common, and the small square at the chest, called a rakusu, is a folded-down robe that carries the old patchwork in miniature. Each community gives its own reasons for its colors, and the reasons are worth asking about. Finally, what stays the same: the cut pieces, the plain dye, the meaning. A robe in any color still says the person inside has taken vows.

segments.voice: Look at one color you're wearing, or one color in the room, and ask quietly: why this one? Chosen, given, inherited, grabbed in a hurry? Then let the question go, and rest your eyes on the color the way a monk might rest a hand on the patchwork of a robe.
Robes and colors. Saffron, maroon, gray and black: different shades in different lands, the same patchwork cut and plain dye from the old rules. Today's word.
Your line: the robe's color. Saffron, maroon, gray or black, the fields of Magadha are sewn into each one. Same time tomorrow.

1376.title: Festivals differ
1376.hook: Vesak, Hanamatsuri, Saga Dawa: one birth, many calendars
1376.howItsDone: Theravada Buddhists keep Vesak with temple visits, lanterns and giving; in Japan, Hanamatsuri is kept by pouring sweet tea over a baby Buddha statue in a flower-covered shrine; Tibetan Buddhists keep Saga Dawa as a month of practice, giving and circling holy places.

segments.voice: Yesterday, robes and colors: saffron, maroon, gray and black, and the rice fields of Magadha sewn into each. Your line was the robe's color.

A small shrine sits on a temple step, its roof covered in fresh flowers. Inside stands a statue of a baby, no taller than a teacup, one hand pointing up to the sky and one down to the earth. A line of children waits with a bamboo ladle. One by one, each dips it in a bowl of sweet tea and pours it gently over the baby's head. Then they giggle and drink a little themselves. It's a birthday party. The guest of honor was born a very long time ago.
screen: `A SHRINE COVERED IN FLOWERS.` → `A BABY POINTING UP AND DOWN.` → `SWEET TEA ON HIS HEAD.`

segments.voice: Why pour water on a baby statue? A Pali discourse, the Discourse on Wonderful and Marvelous Qualities, tells of the Buddha's birth: the newborn stands, takes seven steps, looks out over the quarters and speaks. And two streams of water appear from the sky, one cool and one warm, to bathe him and his mother. The children with the ladle retell that moment with their hands. So the birth is shared. The days are not. First, Vesak, which you met back in year one, kept by Theravada communities in Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia on a full moon in the month of Vesakha. Theravada tradition marks three things on that one day: the birth, the awakening and the passing away. Lanterns, white clothes, temple visits, food given freely. Second, Hanamatsuri, the flower festival, the scene you just heard. In Japan it honors the birth alone, the flowered shrine recalling the garden at Lumbini where tradition says he was born. Korea, China and Vietnam keep their own birthday celebrations by their own calendars, with lanterns and the same bathing of the baby. Third, Saga Dawa, a whole month of practice for Tibetan communities. Its full-moon day honors the awakening and the passing, and in some reckonings the birth as well. People walk circuits around holy places, give to those in need, and some avoid eating meat for the month. So the same birth may be celebrated on several days in one year, by communities that each have good reasons for their count.
screen: `TWO STREAMS OF WATER.` · `VESAK: THREE MOMENTS, ONE DAY.` · `HANAMATSURI: THE FLOWER FESTIVAL.` · `SAGA DAWA: A WHOLE MONTH.` · then, large: `ONE BIRTH, MANY DAYS.`

segments.voice: Call up the little shrine of flowers and the children with the ladle. On each out-breath, picture a little water poured, one cool stream, one warm, over a birth you're grateful for: your own, a child's, a friend's, anyone's.
Festivals differ. Vesak, Hanamatsuri, Saga Dawa: different days, different customs, all honoring the same life. Today's word.

1377.title: Meeting each other
1377.hook: Buddhists of different schools meet in shared councils, such as the World Fellowship of Buddhists
1377.howItsDone: Buddhists of different schools meet in shared bodies such as the World Fellowship of Buddhists, and in local councils and joint celebrations, where they share meals and learn each other's customs while keeping their own traditions.

segments.voice: Yesterday, festivals differ: sweet tea over a baby Buddha, Vesak's lanterns, a month of Saga Dawa. Your line was one birth, many days.

The monks at Kosambi are fighting. In the Pali account, they've split into sides over a point of discipline, and the quarrel has turned to sharp words. The Buddha asks them to stop. They tell him, more or less, to leave it to them. So he does. He walks off alone. On the way, he comes to a small park where three monks are living together, and stops to ask them a question.
screen: `THE QUARREL AT KOSAMBI.` → `HE WALKS OFF ALONE.` → `THREE MONKS IN A PARK.`

segments.voice: The three are Anuruddha, Nandiya and Kimbila. The Buddha asks how they are getting on, and Anuruddha says they live together blending like milk and water, looking at each other with kindly eyes. How? Each one, he says, sets aside what he himself wants and does what the others want. We are different in body, he says, but one in mind. Then he gets practical. Whoever comes back first from the alms round sets out the seats and the water. Whoever comes back last eats what's left and cleans up. Whoever sees the water pot empty fills it, and if it's too heavy, he waves another over, and they lift it together without a word. Seats, water, a heavy pot. Not agreement on every point. Kindness in the chores. Now jump to modern times. Buddhists from different lands and schools, Theravada, Mahayana and Vajrayana, meet in shared bodies such as the World Fellowship of Buddhists. Meeting doesn't merge their schools or settle every question. They sit in one room, share a meal, and learn each other's customs, the robes and festivals and languages of this week. Behind it is a line from the Dhammapada, in Max Müller's old translation: "hatred does not cease by hatred at any time: hatred ceases by love." Kosambi is the warning. The three in the park are the model.
screen: `LIKE MILK AND WATER.` · `SEATS, WATER, A HEAVY POT.` · `COUNCILS ACROSS THE SCHOOLS.` · `HATRED CEASES BY LOVE.` · then, large: `MEETING EACH OTHER.`

Meeting each other. Buddhists of different schools coming together, not to merge, but to live and work side by side, like milk and water. Today's word.

1378.title: Why no ranking
1378.hook: this path teaches schools in their own terms, because each has carried people across
1378.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers point to the Kalama Sutta's test of a teaching by its fruits and the raft simile's teaching that the dhamma is for crossing over, and inter-school bodies meet without asking anyone to give up their own school.

segments.voice: Yesterday, meeting each other: the quarrel at Kosambi, and three monks lifting one water pot. Your line was meeting each other.

The town is called Kesaputta, and its people, the Kalamas, are tired. Teachers keep passing through. Each one arrives, praises his own teaching, and picks apart everyone else's. The next does the same, in reverse. So when the Buddha comes through, the Kalamas ask him straight out: we're confused. Which of these people is telling the truth? It's the perfect moment for him to say: me. He doesn't.
screen: `THE KALAMAS ARE TIRED.` → `EVERY TEACHER PRAISES HIMSELF.` → `WHO IS TELLING THE TRUTH?`

segments.voice: First, the test, which you met back in year one. In the Kalama Sutta, the Buddha says it makes sense that they're unsure, and tells them not to settle it by report, by tradition, by scripture, by clever reasoning, or by the standing of the teacher. Look at what a teaching does. When you know for yourselves that something leads to greed, hatred and confusion, to harm and suffering, set it aside. When you know it leads to welfare and happiness, take it up. Test the fruit. Second, the raft. In another discourse, the Buddha compares his teaching to a raft. A man faces a wide river, danger on this side and safety on the far side. He binds a raft from sticks and grass and paddles across. Should he then carry it on his head forever? No. The teaching is for crossing over, not for holding on to. Third, honest history. Schools have argued. Some Mahayana texts used a dismissive name for other paths, Hinayana, the lesser vehicle. Theravada keeps an old book of debates, the Kathavatthu, setting out its answers to views held by other schools. Disagreement is real and long. That's exactly why this path teaches each school in its own terms, the way its own teachers would explain it, and doesn't pick a winner. Fourth, the reason. Each of these schools has been a raft. Monks in Thai forests, Zen students in Kyoto, grandmothers chanting in Lhasa, families at a Korean temple: their rafts look different, and people have crossed on all of them. Ranking the rafts doesn't get anyone across.
screen: `TEST THE FRUIT.` · `THE RAFT IS FOR CROSSING.` · `THE SCHOOLS HAVE ARGUED.` · `EACH RAFT HAS CARRIED PEOPLE.` · then, large: `NO RANKING.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one school you've met this year that you'll probably never join; maybe its chanting, its rules or its way of sitting isn't your style. Picture one person it has carried, a nun, a farmer, a grandmother, a teenager in a temple courtyard, reaching the far bank on that raft. Honor it quietly, without needing to climb aboard.
Why no ranking. Because each school has carried people across, this path teaches every one in its own terms and picks no winner. Today's word.
Your line: no ranking. Learning how each raft floats does more than ranking them. See you tomorrow.

1379.title: Your door among the schools
1379.hook: where you feel at home, and why that doesn't make others wrong
1379.howItsDone: A Buddhist may practice within one school or lineage, with its own teachers, texts and customs, while visiting, learning from and celebrating with other schools.

segments.voice: Yesterday, why no ranking: the tired Kalamas, the test of the fruit, and the raft that's for crossing. Your line was no ranking.

A householder named Dasama, from the town of Atthakanagara, goes out of his way to find Ananda, the Buddha's old attendant. He asks a simple question: is there one teaching that opens the way to freedom? Ananda gives him eleven, one after another: ways of meditating, ways of loving, ways of letting the mind grow wide and still. Dasama is delighted. He was looking for one door, and he has been shown a house full of them.
screen: `DASAMA ASKS FOR ONE DOOR.` → `ANANDA GIVES ELEVEN.` → `A HOUSE FULL OF DOORS.`

segments.voice: Here is what Dasama says, in the Pali discourse that bears his town's name. Suppose a man's house has eleven doors, and the house catches fire. He could get out safely through any one of them. In the same way, he says, I can find my way out through any one of these eleven doors. Notice what he doesn't say. He doesn't call the other ten fake, or tear them down once he's out. He just needs one to walk through. Careful, though: the text is about kinds of meditation, not about schools. But the picture travels well. Second, the home. Over this block you've met Theravada and Mahayana, the arahant and the bodhisattva, chanting and silence, sudden and gradual, three canons and four languages. Some of it may have felt like home: a robe color, a style of sitting, a text that spoke to you. Or none of it yet, which is also fine. Third, the wall. A home has a door you use. A wall is built to keep others out. Choosing where you feel at home doesn't require deciding everyone else is in the wrong house. Dasama's eleven doors all lead out of the same fire. Fourth, the Kalamas again: you can test a door by what it does for you, and still honor the doors that work for others. Some teachers tell students to go deep in one practice rather than tasting all of them forever. That's a door. Walking through it with respect for the other ten is the difference between a home and a wall.
screen: `A HOUSE WITH ELEVEN DOORS.` · `WHAT FELT LIKE HOME?` · `A DOOR IS NOT A WALL.` · `GO DEEP, HONOR THE REST.` · then, large: `A HOME, NOT A WALL.`

segments.voice: Look back over the schools and practices of these weeks and ask, without pushing: where did something in me relax? A chant, a silence, a story, a robe, a teacher's line. Let one come forward, or let it be that none has yet, and if one does, give it a single quiet sentence that begins: I feel at home in.
Your door among the schools. The school or practice that feels like home, chosen without walling anyone else out. Today's word.
screen: `YOUR DOOR AMONG THE SCHOOLS — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: a home, not a wall. The week closes: three canons, four languages, robes and colors, festivals, meeting each other, no ranking, and your door. I'll be here tomorrow.
